content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method to remove blind multi-distribution noise. The key idea of this work is to deal with the trade-off between specialization and generalization while training deep denoisers. The first contribution is an adaptive sampling strategy, which leads the denoisers to have a better generalization of different noise parameters. The second contribution lies in the polynomial approximation of specification-loss landscape, which can reduce the computational costs to a great deal. The experiments mainly show the performance improvements over uniform sampling strategy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The overall writing of this work is clear and easy to follow.
+ It is significant and meaningful to discuss the trade-off of specialization and generalization, in the field of image denoising.
+ The formulation of specification-loss landscape is clear, which well defines the specification of the functions to solve a given task.

Weakness:
- I am afraid that the claimed contributions are insufficient for publishing in ICLR. The adaptive training strategy seems trivial, and the specification-loss approximation looks more like a sparser parameter sampling way, compared to the dense loss (I assume that dense loss is still discontinuous).
- My biggest concern is about the practicality of this work. First, though the authors claim that they deal with blind denoising. However, the ranges of each noise parameters are still wanted. Otherwise, it may waste large computational cost to guarantee the range cover the targeted noisy images. Second, the noise models used in this paper contain simple two or three noise components, but existing works show that real noisy contains more complex components [1,2]. The computation costs for such brute-force searching strategy of ideal loss (including the approximation) increase exponentially, and prevent this work from applying in more complexly distributed noise. I wonder how it can work to solve noise removal tasks in real scenarios.
[1] Rethinking noise synthesis and modeling in raw denoising, ICCV 2021
[2] A Physics-based Noise Formation Model for Extreme Low-light Raw Denoising, CVPR 2020
- The experiments are not sufficient. Maybe more noise models like gaussian mixture or real-world noise model can be considered. In addition, this paper only compares the proposed methods with uniform sampling strategy. However, state-of-the-art image denoising methods should be compared.
- Figure 1 is recommended to be simplified, for the information conveyed by Fig 1 is limited and is not worthy of such space. 
- Typo: below Equation (1), there are two ‘the’s in the sentence.

Clarity: good
Quality: Fair (Especially the exeriments)
Novelty: Fair
Reproducibility: Good

content.title: Response to reviewer 2
content.comment:
- I am afraid that the claimed contributions are insufficient for publishing in ICLR. The adaptive training strategy seems trivial, and the specification-loss approximation looks more like a sparser parameter sampling way, compared to the dense loss (I assume that dense loss is still discontinuous).
  - With respect, we believe contributions like ours are exactly what should be published at ICLR. We introduce a new insight — the specification–loss landscape is highly regular; we propose a simple, easy-to-understand algorithm based on this insight — one form an accurate polynomial approximation this landscape using sparse samples and use this approximation to guide training; and we show that this algorithm has a large impact on performance — we reduce training times by 100x.
  - We're unsure what the reviewer means by "sparser parameter sampling way" and that the "dense loss is still discontinuous". Densely sampled loss landscapes are shown in Figures 2 and 7 and Proposition 1 proves that (in the large signal regime) the poisson-gaussian loss is not only continuous but linear.
- My biggest concern is about the practicality of this work. First, though the authors claim that they deal with blind denoising. However, the ranges of each noise parameters are still wanted. Otherwise, it may waste large computational cost to guarantee the range cover the targeted noisy images. 
  - Indeed our method requires knowing the range of parameters a denoiser may expect to see. However, this is a weak assumption and the set of possible ranges one needs to select scales linearly with the number of parameters. 
- Second, the noise models used in this paper contain simple two or three noise components, but existing works show that real noisy contains more complex components [1,2]. The computation costs for such brute-force searching strategy of ideal loss (including the approximation) increase exponentially, and prevent this work from applying in more complexly distributed noise. I wonder how it can work to solve noise removal tasks in real scenarios.
  - Real-world noise can indeed be quite complicated with many components. Fortunately, the number of samples required to fit a quadratic approximation of the loss landscape scales quadratically, not exponentially, with the number of noise components/specifications n. Please see the Appendix E in the revision.
- Maybe more noise models like gaussian mixture or real-world noise model can be considered. 
  - With respect, we feel 4 noise distributions (Poisson-Gaussian, Poisson-Speckle, Speckle-Gaussian, Speckle-Poisson-Gaussian) is adequate to validate our training strategy.
- The paper only compares the proposed methods with uniform sampling strategy. 
  - Our adaptive training method was compared extensively to the only other universal denoiser strategy we are aware of [3], which is represented by the “adaptive dense sampling” results throughout our paper. Additional quantitative results are presented in Appendix D of the revision.
- However, state-of-the-art image denoising methods should be compared.
  - Our adaptive training method is agnostic to the denoiser’s network architecture. As DnCNN [4] is still widely used in practice (it is significantly more efficient than more recent network architectures like DrUNET [5] or transformers [6]), we felt it was the most appropriate architecture on which to demonstrate our method. (Even with the lightweight DnCNN architecture, training the “ideal” baselines we compare against took over 100 GPU days.)

 [1] Zhang et al. Rethinking noise synthesis and modeling in raw denoising [2] Wei et al. A Physics-based Noise Formation Model for Extreme Low-light Raw Denoising [3] Chan et al.  One Size Fits All: Can We Train One Denoiser for All Noise Levels? [4] Zhang et al. Beyond a gaussian denoiser: Residual learning of deep cnn for image denoising [5] Zhang et al. Plug-and-Play Image Restoration with Deep Denoiser Prior [6] Liang et al. SwinIR: Image Restoration Using Swin Transformer

content.title: Response to R1
content.comment:
- It is said that training is done using multiple datasets, but it is not specifically stated how it was curated.
  - We have added additional info on augmentation etc. to section 5.2.
- There is no experiment on real mixed noise that occurs in the real environment.
  - Poisson-gaussian noise is commonly used as a model for real mixed noise in the environment, see [1]. Furthermore, our method is agnostic to the noise model and can naturally be extended to be applied to more complex parameterized noise models, like [2].
- There is no experiment using color images.
  - The primary motivation for our work was denoising images from coherent imaging systems, which suffer from speckle and do not have color image outputs. Furthermore, grayscale denoising is a strictly more difficult problem than color image denoising — one can't take advantage of inter-channel correlations.
- There are no quantitative and qualitative comparisons with recent denoising techniques.
  - Our adaptive training methodology, which is the focus of this work, was compared extensively to the only other universal denoiser strategy we are aware of [6], which is represented by the “adaptive dense sampling” results throughout our paper. Additional quantitative results are presented in Appendix D of the revision.
  - Our adaptive denoiser training strategy is agnostic to the denoiser’s network architecture. As DnCNN [3] is still widely used in practice (it is significantly more efficient than more recent network architectures like DrUNET [4] or transformers [5]), we felt it was the most appropriate architecture on which to demonstrate our method. (Even with the lightweight DnCNN architecture, training the “ideal” baselines we compare against took over 100 GPU days.)
- The only qualitative results are in Figure 6. Very little experimentation.
  - We have added additional qualitative results to the appendix. 

[1] Foi et al. Practical Poissonian-Gaussian Noise Modeling and Fitting for Single-Image Raw-Data [2] Wei et al. A Physics-based Noise Formation Model for Extreme Low-light Raw Denoising [3] Zhang et al. Beyond a gaussian denoiser: Residual learning of deep cnn for image denoising [4] Zhang et al. Plug-and-Play Image Restoration with Deep Denoiser Prior [5] Liang et al. SwinIR: Image Restoration Using Swin Transformer [6] Chan et al One Size Fits All: Can We Train One Denoiser for All Noise Levels?
